rubric: PYTHON AS A FIRST LANGUAGE / DICTIONARIES AND TUPLES / CHAPTER 11

slides.title: Tuples
slides.main: Immutability is a useful limit: a tuple's contents can't be spoiled by accident.

items.title: Tuple
items.sub: An ordered collection that can't be changed

items.title: Dict key
items.sub: Composite key: a table over two attributes

body.text: You've met tuples already: each pair from enumerate, zip, and items() is a tuple.

slides.title: Creating a tuple
slides.sub: The comma creates a tuple, not the parentheses
slides.main: One element needs a trailing comma: (1,) is a tuple, (1) is just a number.

body.text:
t = (1, 2, 3)
point = 4, 5          # parentheses are optional
one = (1,)            # the comma is needed
print(type((1)), type(one))
tuple(list) and tuple(string) turn a collection into a tuple.

slides.title: What a tuple can do
slides.sub: Everything that doesn't change, as with a list
slides.main: No editing methods: no append, remove, or sort.

body.text:
t = (10, 20, 30)
print(t[0], t[-1], t[1:], len(t), 20 in t)
t[0] = 99                # TypeError

10 30 (20, 30) 3 True
TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

slides.title: To change means to rebuild
slides.sub: Plus, multiplication, slices: a new tuple
slides.main: Immutability guards against edits via a second reference; only such data fits as keys.

slides.title: Unpacking
slides.sub: As many names on the left as elements
slides.main: A star gathers the extras into a list; an underscore means "value not needed".

body.text:
a, b = (1, 2)
first, *rest = [10, 20, 30]
x, _ = ("needed", "extra")
print(a, b, first, rest)

slides.title: Swapping values
slides.main: The right side is fully evaluated before assignment, so there is no mix-up.

body.text:
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)
Works with any number of values: a, b, c = b, c, a is a circular shift.

slides.title: Returning several values
slides.sub: return a, b is a tuple
slides.main: The function returned one tuple, and the caller unpacked it into two variables.

slides.title: Tuples all around us
slides.sub: enumerate, zip, and items() give tuples
slides.main: No magic: the loop takes the next tuple and spreads it across variables.

body.text: Not unpacked: the variable holds the whole tuple, and parts are reached by index: pair[1].

slides.title: Tuple as a key
slides.main: A list can't be a key, a tuple can: a dict becomes a table over two attributes.

body.text:
field = {}
field[(0, 0)] = "X"
field[(1, 2)] = "O"
print(field[(1, 2)])
print((0, 1) in field)

slides.title: List or tuple
slides.sub: A homogeneous collection or a fixed-structure record
slides.main: If nobody should write to the data, use a tuple; if you keep appending, a list.

body.text:
grades = [5, 4, 5]               # list
person = ("Anya", 20, "Tver")    # record tuple
print(tuple(grades), list(person))

cells.title: list
cells.sub: Grades, file names: the length varies

cells.title: tuple
cells.sub: Name, age, city: position has meaning

slides.title: Comparing and sorting
slides.sub: Left to right: first elements, then second
slides.main: A tuple key sorts by several attributes: the first is main, the second breaks ties.

body.text:
print((1, 5) < (2, 0), (1, 5) < (1, 7))
people = [("Anya", 20), ("Borya", 30), ("Vera", 20)]

def by_key(p):
    return -p[1], p[0]

print(sorted(people, key=by_key))

slides.title: Pitfalls
slides.sub: The comma, shallowness, the number of names
slides.main: Immutability is shallow: a list inside a tuple can still be changed.

body.text:
not_tuple = (5)        # just a number
t = (1, [2, 3])
t[1].append(4)          # the list inside can change!
print(t)
# a, b = (1, 2, 3)      # ValueError: too many values to unpack
Such a tuple can't be a dict key; += on a tuple creates a new one.

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: We're done with Python's basic containers: lists, dicts, and tuples.

items.sub: The comma creates; * gathers the extras

items.sub: Left to right; a tuple key for sorting

body.text: A list is for a homogeneous collection, a tuple is for a fixed-structure record.
